summary: Bits are tiny, fast, and tricky. The whole topic boils down to four operations (AND for masking, OR for setting, XOR for toggling/comparing, shift for positioning) and one identity that powers half the problems: a ^ a = 0. Once you internalise XOR's pairing magic and the bit-by-bit accumulation pattern (loop i = 0..30, ask 'how many numbers have bit i set?'), 80% of bit problems reduce to one or two passes.

thoughtProcess.title: 1. Need to ISOLATE bit i? AND with a mask.
thoughtProcess.body: (x >> i) & 1 tells you bit i. (x & (1 << i)) != 0 is the equivalent boolean form. Always parenthesise the shift — operator precedence will bite you.

thoughtProcess.title: 2. Need to SET / CLEAR / TOGGLE bit i?
thoughtProcess.body: Set: x | (1 << i). Clear: x & ~(1 << i). Toggle: x ^ (1 << i). Memorise the trio — every bit problem uses at least one.

thoughtProcess.title: 3. Looking for the lonely element? Think XOR.
thoughtProcess.body: Because a ^ a = 0 and a ^ 0 = a, XOR-folding an array cancels everything that appears in pairs. The leftover IS the answer. Generalises with bit-counts when elements appear 3 times instead of 2.

thoughtProcess.title: 4. Counting something across an array of integers?
thoughtProcess.body: Loop bit position i from 0 to 30. For each i, count how many numbers have bit i set (call it c). Use c, (N - c), or c * (N - c) depending on whether you want OR-of-subarray, AND-of-subarray, or sum-of-XOR-pairs. This 'per-bit pass' trick converts O(N^2) over numbers into O(31 * N).

thoughtProcess.title: 5. Want a power of 2? n & (n - 1) == 0.
thoughtProcess.body: Powers of two have exactly one bit set; n - 1 flips that bit and everything below. ANDing them gives 0. Also: lowest set bit = n & -n. Count set bits with the Brian-Kernighan trick: n &= (n - 1) drops one bit per step.

thoughtProcess.title: 6. Overflow with shifts.
thoughtProcess.body: 1 << 31 is negative in int. Use 1L << i when i can reach 31. Magic-number-style problems with base-5 or base-7 also overflow int around N = 12 — use long upfront.

thoughtProcess.title: 7. Building a k-bit mask? Prefer (1 << k) - 1, and watch k = 32.
thoughtProcess.body: A contiguous low mask of k ones is (1 << k) - 1: k=4 gives 0b1111 = 15. But (1 << 32) is undefined-shift territory in Java — the shift count is taken mod 32, so 1 << 32 == 1 << 0 == 1, NOT 0. For all 32 bits use -1 (0xFFFFFFFF), and use (int)((1L << k) - 1) when k can reach 32. High-bit mask: ~((1 << k) - 1).

thoughtProcess.title: 8. Reasoning about XOR? Treat each bit column as independent addition mod 2.
thoughtProcess.body: XOR is per-bit addition without carry. Bit i of a^b^c depends ONLY on bit i of a, b, c — never on neighbours. This independence justifies per-bit contribution counting in AND/OR/XOR-over-subarray problems: solve each of the 31 columns in isolation, then weight column i by (1 << i) and sum.

commonMistakes.title: Missing parentheses around shift
commonMistakes.why: != binds tighter than &. The wrong version evaluates 1 << i != 0 first (which is true) then ANDs with x. Always parenthesise the whole mask-test.

commonMistakes.title: Using int for 1 << 31
commonMistakes.wrong: int mask = 1 << 31;  // becomes Integer.MIN_VALUE, surprising in arithmetic
commonMistakes.why: 1 << 31 is the sign bit in int and prints as -2147483648. Comparisons and modular arithmetic break silently.

commonMistakes.title: XOR-find-lonely written with HashSet
commonMistakes.wrong: Set<Integer> s = new HashSet<>(); for (int x : A) if (!s.add(x)) s.remove(x);
commonMistakes.right: int x = 0; for (int v : A) x ^= v; return x;
commonMistakes.why: The HashSet version is O(N) time but O(N) space. XOR is O(N) time, O(1) space — and elegant.

commonMistakes.title: Single Number II (every other appears 3x) with XOR alone
commonMistakes.wrong: int x = 0; for (int v : A) x ^= v;
commonMistakes.why: XOR only cancels pairs (mod 2). When duplicates appear 3 times, you need a per-bit mod-3 sum.

commonMistakes.title: Magic number / base-N expansion in int
commonMistakes.wrong:
int answer = 0, pow = 1;
while (N > 0) { if ((N & 1) == 1) answer += pow; pow *= 5; N >>= 1; }
commonMistakes.right:
long answer = 0, pow = 1;
while (N > 0) { if ((N & 1) == 1) answer += pow; pow *= 5; N >>= 1; }
commonMistakes.why: 5^14 overflows int. Promote both answer and pow to long.

commonMistakes.title: Subarray-OR counted by brute O(N^2)
commonMistakes.wrong: for (int i = 0; i < N; i++) for (int j = i; j < N; j++) if (OR(i..j) == 1) ++count;
commonMistakes.right:
// Count subarrays whose OR is 0: those entirely inside runs of 0s.
// Total subarrays = N*(N+1)/2; answer = total - sum over runs of len L of L*(L+1)/2.
commonMistakes.why: Direct enumeration is O(N^2). Complement counting using runs of zeros is O(N).

commonMistakes.title: Unmasked arithmetic shift driving a loop
commonMistakes.wrong: while (n != 0) { c += n & 1; n >>= 1; }   // never ends for n < 0
commonMistakes.right: for (int i = 0; i < 32; i++) c += (n >>> i) & 1;   // or loop exactly 32 times
commonMistakes.why: (v >> i) & 1 is actually SAFE — the & 1 discards the sign-extended high bits, so it equals bit i for any v. The real hazard is an unmasked arithmetic shift used as the loop value: for negative n, >> keeps shifting in 1s and n >>= 1 never reaches 0. Use >>> or a fixed 32 iterations.

commonMistakes.title: Comparing a bit test to 1 instead of to the mask
commonMistakes.wrong: if ((A & (1 << i)) == 1) { ... }  // only ever true for i == 0
commonMistakes.why: A & (1 << i) yields 0 or (1 << i) — which equals 1 only when i is 0. Compare against 0 (!= 0), or shift the bit down to position 0 first.

commonMistakes.title: Weighting a bit contribution with an int shift
commonMistakes.wrong: long contrib = count * (1 << i);   // 1 << i overflows int at i >= 31
commonMistakes.right: long contrib = count * (1L << i);  // 1L keeps the shift in 64-bit
commonMistakes.why: 1 << i is evaluated in int first and overflows/goes negative at i = 31 before widening to long. The literal must be 1L. Widening the target variable doesn't fix an already-overflowed int expression.

keyPatterns.name: Single-Bit Get / Set / Clear / Toggle
keyPatterns.when: Any problem that needs to manipulate one bit at a known position.

keyPatterns.name: Population Count (Brian Kernighan)
keyPatterns.when: Count set bits in an integer.

keyPatterns.name: XOR-Fold Lonely Element
keyPatterns.when: All elements appear in pairs except one.

keyPatterns.name: Per-Bit Accumulation (mod 3)
keyPatterns.when: Every element appears 3 times except one. Same skeleton for many 'find unique via bits' variants.

keyPatterns.name: XOR Partition (two unique elements)
keyPatterns.when: Two elements appear once, the rest in pairs. Use the XOR of all to isolate a differing bit, then partition.

keyPatterns.name: Base-N Magic Number
keyPatterns.when: Encode N as a sum of distinct powers of base-K (typically K = 5 for magic numbers).

keyPatterns.name: Complement Counting on Runs
keyPatterns.when: Count subarrays whose OR is at least 1 — count zero-OR ones (runs of zeros) and subtract.

keyPatterns.name: Bit-Sum Trick for Subarray OR
keyPatterns.when: Sum over all subarrays of (OR of subarray). For each bit i, count subarrays where bit i appears at least once: contribute (1 << i) * thatCount.

keyPatterns.name: Isolate / Strip the Lowest Set Bit
keyPatterns.when: You need the value/position of the least-significant 1, or want to iterate set bits one at a time.

keyPatterns.name: Iterate All Subsets of a Mask
keyPatterns.when: Enumerate every submask of a bitmask (subset-sum / bitmask DP).

edgeCases: i = 31 — the shift amount equals the sign bit position. Use 1L << i if you need a positive mask.
Empty array for XOR-fold returns 0 — make sure 0 is a valid answer or guard length.
Negative numbers in 'Single Number III' — XOR-of-differing-bit still works because two's complement preserves XOR identity.
n = 0 in popcount — loop never enters, returns 0.
N = 1 in nth magic number — return 5.
All zeros for Subarrays-with-OR-1 — answer is 0, the run-length sum equals N*(N+1)/2.
Subarray-OR with very long arrays — running contribution can exceed int even when bits don't; use long.
Find-two-missing problems with sum overflow — use the XOR formulation (or use long for the sum formulation).
Help-from-Sam style staircase problems — power-of-2 transitions, use 1L when N exceeds 30.

Popcount via arithmetic shift (while(n!=0){c+=n&1; n>>=1;}) loops forever for n < 0 — use >>> or loop 32 times. (Brian-Kernighan's n &= (n-1) is fine: it clears one set bit per step and ends in <= 32 iterations, no guard needed.)
n & -n on n = 0 returns 0 (no lowest set bit) — guard before using it as a bit position/divisor.
n & -n on Integer.MIN_VALUE returns Integer.MIN_VALUE (only the sign bit set) — store in long if you do arithmetic with it.
Shift amounts are taken mod 32 for int (mod 64 for long): x << 32 == x, not 0.
Integer.numberOfTrailingZeros(0) and numberOfLeadingZeros(0) both return 32 — the all-zero input is the boundary case.
Submask enumeration sub = (sub-1) & mask stops at sub == 0, so the empty subset is never visited inside the loop — handle separately.
